evidence_quotes.quote: The major aim of the paper is to reconstruct the history of water management that led to the current water delivery system in Cameroon using the exploratory approach of data analysis supported with diagrams.
Water management is done by the declaration of decrees from time to time, however a comprehensive water law does not exist even to date (Kouam et al., 2006).
After the takeover of water supply by the private sector, SNEC broke into the Cameroon Water Utilities (CAMWATER) and La Camerounaise des Eaux (CDE).

The primary data were generated through personal observations. The secondary data were derived from the records of Cameroon National Assembly, Cameroon National Archives in Buea and Yaounde, and the government of Cameroon.

In Cameroon, the first two components – water policy and water law are non-existent; and the third component exits but is not properly developed should the other two components had evolved historically.

criterion_notes.c1: Broadly examines the history and institutional organization of domestic drinking water provisioning and delivery in Cameroon, referencing urban utility supply, informal vendors, and rural/community water projects.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it surveys legal, administrative, and institutional frameworks for water management in Cameroon from pre-colonial times to 2010 (colonial deliberations, water resource statutes, executive decrees, ministerial structures, and the split of SNEC into CAMWATER and CDE). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow = no) because it presents unanalysed macro-governance history, statutory/decree inventories primarily concerning general water resource control and industrial/mineral abstraction, inter-ministerial organigrams, and secondary summaries of generic community self-help project delivery rather than analysing a specific rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for lacking empirical access evidence (c3, c4, c5).
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence or systematic synthesis on service access. Although the authors mention archival sources and unsystematic personal observations, the text consists of a chronological doctrinal summary of statutes and decrees, institutional organigrams, secondary summaries of two community water projects from Njoh (2002, 2006), a two-row archival table of 1999 municipal council debt to SNEC, and normative policy commentary; there is no empirical methodology, sampling, primary qualitative/quantitative data analysis, or systematic synthesis -> exclude as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not empirically measure or report household- or community-level service access, connection, continuity, quantity, or affordability outcomes; references to water shortages, informal jerry-can prices, backyard wells, and secondary project completion are purely descriptive background.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not define an empirical study population/sample, analytical unit for access outcomes, or identifiable empirical study design linking a specific institutional exposure to measured service access outcomes.

exposure: Historical evolution of national water management laws, administrative decrees, ministerial structures, and utility arrangements in Cameroon
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the paper discusses drinking water delivery in Cameroon and surveys national legal, administrative, and institutional structures from pre-colonial times to 2010, it is a descriptive historical-doctrinal and macro-governance policy overview relying on statutory/decree summaries, conceptual organigrams, secondary summaries of Njoh (2002, 2006), two municipal council debt figures from 1999, and casual personal observations without an identifiable empirical method, sample, or measured service-access outcome. Under Criterion 2, it satisfies the plain broad wording (macro-legal/institutional review) but fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism scope; under both readings the overall decision is exclude due to the absence of empirical access evidence.
